teile.einleitung: T helper cells are white blood cells that direct the immune system. They hardly kill any germs themselves, but they give other defence cells the signals they need. Without them, the defence collapses.
wichtigste: T helper cells carry the co-receptor CD4.
They recognise fragments of germs on MHC class II molecules.
Th1 cells activate scavenger cells, Th2 cells help against worms.
Follicular T helper cells support B cells in the lymph nodes.
Regulatory T cells dampen immune reactions.
HIV attacks T helper cells in particular.
Interleukin-2 is an important growth factor for T cells.

abschnitte.text: T helper cells are also called CD4-positive T cells, after their surface molecule **CD4**. Their **T cell receptor** recognises small pieces of protein that other cells display on **MHC class II molecules**. These molecules mainly carry fragments of proteins that have been taken in, for example from bacteria. The co-receptor CD4 stabilises the bond with this **antigen-presenting cell**.

Once activated, T helper cells release messenger substances, the **interleukins**. **Interleukin-2** is especially important, as it encourages T cells to multiply strongly. In this way a large number of suitable defence cells is created in a short time. The helper cells act like an operations control centre that decides which kind of defence is needed.

**Th1 cells** mainly activate scavenger cells, the **macrophages**. This helps to kill germs that live inside cells, such as tuberculosis bacteria. **Th2 cells** release interleukin-4, interleukin-5 and interleukin-13. They promote the production of IgE and the defence against worms, but are also involved in **allergies**. **Follicular T helper cells** travel to the lymph nodes and help the **B cells** there to make better antibodies.

**Regulatory T cells** have a special job: they **dampen** immune reactions. In this way they slow down defence responses that go too far. They help to prevent **autoimmune diseases**, in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissue.

The **HI virus** uses the CD4 molecule as a way in and gradually destroys the T helper cells. Healthy people have about 500 to 1,500 CD4 cells per microlitre of blood. If the count falls **below 200**, it is called **AIDS**. Then the risk of serious infections rises sharply. With today's medicines the virus can be kept well under control.

gewusst: Because HIV attacks the operations control centre of the immune system, otherwise harmless germs can become dangerous.
The abbreviation CD stands for “Cluster of Differentiation”, a numbering system for surface molecules.

teile.einleitung: Swissmedic is the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products. It checks whether medicines and medical devices are safe, effective and of good quality before they may be sold in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Swissmedic has existed since 2002.
Its predecessor was the Intercantonal Office for the Control of Medicines (IKS).
The basis is the Therapeutic Products Act (HMG).
Swissmedic monitors side effects even after approval.
The Federal Office of Public Health decides on the prices of medicines.
Medicines in category E can be sold freely.

abschnitte.text: Until 2001, medicines were checked by the **Intercantonal Office for the Control of Medicines** (IKS), a joint body of the cantons. In 2002 **Swissmedic** began its work together with the new **Therapeutic Products Act** (HMG). The law regulates the approval, manufacture, supply and monitoring of medicines and medical devices. Swissmedic is based in Bern.

Before a new medicine may be sold, Swissmedic checks its **safety**, **effectiveness** and **quality**. Even after approval, rare side effects can appear. Professionals and patients report suspected cases, and Swissmedic evaluates them. This task is called **pharmacovigilance**. The price of a medicine and whether health insurance pays for it are decided instead by the **Federal Office of Public Health**.

Medicines are sorted into **supply categories**. For some you need a doctor's prescription. Others are only available at a pharmacy or chemist's with expert advice. Medicines in **category E**, such as certain lozenges, may also be sold in shops without expert advice. This makes sure that strong medicines are used correctly.

Swissmedic regularly warns against ordering from unknown **online shops** abroad. Many medicines offered there are **fakes** with the wrong dose or dangerous ingredients. Customs often stops such parcels. It is safer to get medicines from a pharmacy or from a doctor.

gewusst: Swissmedic is also responsible for medical devices, for example plasters or blood sugar meters.
Fake medicines often look exactly the same as the real ones.

teile.einleitung: Thalassaemia is an inherited disease of the blood. In it the body makes too little of the building blocks from which the red blood pigment haemoglobin is made. Depending on the form, you hardly notice it, or you need treatment for life.
wichtigste: In thalassaemia too few globin chains are made, but their shape is usually normal.
The name comes from the Greek word “thalassa” for sea, because the disease was first described in people from the Mediterranean region.
Small, pale red blood cells are typical.
The severe form of beta thalassaemia is also called Cooley's anaemia.
Many blood transfusions lead to iron overload in the body.
A normal ferritin level helps to tell mild thalassaemia from iron deficiency.

abschnitte.titel: What is missing in the blood
abschnitte.text: The **haemoglobin** in the red blood cells carries oxygen. It is made of protein chains, the **globin chains**, and of iron. In adults these are mainly two alpha chains and two beta chains. In thalassaemia, too little of one of these kinds of chain is made. If beta chains are missing, it is called **beta thalassaemia**, and if alpha chains are missing, **alpha thalassaemia**.

The building instructions for the chains are in the genes. A person normally has **four genes** for the alpha chain, two on each of the two chromosomes 16. The more of these that fail, the more severe the alpha thalassaemia. For the beta chain there are two genes. If only one is altered, the mild **thalassaemia minor** results, and if both are altered, the severe **thalassaemia major**.

In a blood count you see **small and pale** red blood cells, often also so-called target cells. This looks similar to iron deficiency. The difference shows in the **ferritin**, the stored iron: in thalassaemia it is normal or raised, in iron deficiency low. In beta thalassaemia minor the proportion of **HbA2** is also raised, usually above 3.5 per cent.

The mild form usually needs no treatment. The severe form, described in 1925 by the doctor Thomas Cooley, is therefore also called **Cooley's anaemia**. People with it often need regular **blood transfusions** even as children. With every transfusion, iron enters the body, and it is hardly excreted. Against this **iron overload** they take medicines called iron chelators. A stem cell transplant can cure the disease in some cases.

gewusst: Thalassaemia is especially common where malaria used to be widespread, because carriers are slightly better protected against malaria.
Many people with thalassaemia minor do not even know that they have this trait.

teile.einleitung: The sense of touch is the sense with which we feel touch, pressure, warmth, cold and pain through the skin. It helps you, for example, to feel whether something is hot or cold. Its sense organ is the skin, our largest organ.
wichtigste: With the sense of touch we feel touch, pressure, vibration, warmth and cold through the skin.
It helps you to feel whether something is hot or cold.
In the skin lie different sensory cells, the receptors.
Fingertips, lips and tongue are especially sensitive.
The sense of touch is the first sense to develop in an unborn child.
Pain warns us of injuries.
Blind people read Braille with their sense of touch.

abschnitte.titel: What is the sense of touch?
abschnitte.text: The **sense of touch** is one of the five classic senses. Experts also speak of **haptic perception**. It tells us whether something is rough or smooth, soft or hard, wet or dry. Often the sensing of temperature and pain are counted as part of it too. Its sense organ is the skin, which in adults is about 1.5 to 2 square metres in size.

In the skin lie different **receptors**, each of which reacts to something particular. Some report light touch, others strong pressure or vibration. **Thermoreceptors** report warmth and cold, which is why you feel whether the soup is hot. Free nerve endings report pain. There are also nerves at the roots of the hairs, which is why you feel it when an insect crawls over your arm.

The touch receptors are not spread out evenly. There are especially many in the **fingertips**, the lips and the tongue. On the back they lie much further apart. You can test this: touch someone with two pencil points. On a finger you feel two points, on the back often only one. This test is called the **two-point test**.

The sense of touch is the first sense to develop, just a few weeks after conception in the womb. Newborns explore the world with their hands and mouth. Touches such as cuddling calm them and are very important for babies' development. In the process the body releases the hormone **oxytocin**. It strengthens the feeling of closeness and trust.

abschnitte.titel: The sense of touch in everyday life
abschnitte.text: With the sense of touch we button up shirts and find the light switch in the dark. **Pain** warns us so that we take our hand off the hot cooker ring in time. Blind people read **Braille**, made of raised dots and invented by the Frenchman Louis Braille. Smartphones also use the sense of touch when they vibrate. Many animals, such as cats with their whiskers, also feel very finely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sensory cell that detects a particular stimulus.
A sensory cell in the skin that feels warmth or cold.
To do with touching and feeling.
A writing system of dots for blind people, which is read with the fingers.

gewusst: Louis Braille invented his dot writing system while still a teenager.
An adult's skin weighs several kilograms, which makes it the heaviest organ.
You can hardly tickle yourself, because the brain predicts your own movement.

teile.einleitung: Sweet is one of the basic tastes that we detect with our tongue. Almost everyone likes sweet things from a very young age. The sweet taste tells the body that a food contains energy.
wichtigste: Sugar makes food sweet.
Sweet is one of the basic tastes.
Even babies like sweet things especially.
Sweet tells the body: there is energy in here.
Ripe fruits such as bananas taste especially sweet.
You should brush your teeth after eating sweet things.

abschnitte.text: With our tongue we taste **sweet**, **sour**, **salty**, **bitter** and **umami**, a savoury taste. For this there are many tiny **taste buds** on the tongue. **Sugar** is what tastes sweet above all. It is found in fruit, honey and sweets. Even babies like the sweet taste especially.

Sugar gives the body **energy**, for example for the muscles and the brain. The sweet taste is therefore a signal: there is energy in here. In the past this helped people to find nourishing fruit. Today sweet things are everywhere, so you should only eat them in moderation.

As a fruit **ripens**, it produces more sugar and its taste becomes sweeter. Unripe fruit often tastes sour or tart. Ripe **bananas** contain a lot of sugar and so taste especially sweet. Ripe strawberries, grapes or apples also taste sweeter than unripe ones.

In warm countries a lot of sugar is made from **sugar cane**. This is a tall grass with sweet juice. In Switzerland sugar is made from **sugar beet**. **Maple syrup** is made from the sap of the **sugar maple**. The sap is boiled for a long time until a sweet syrup is left. **Honey** is sweet too, and bees make it from flower nectar.

In the mouth live **bacteria** that turn sugar into acid. This acid can make holes in the teeth, which is called **tooth decay**. That is why you should **brush your teeth** after eating sweets. Drinking water also helps to wash away leftover sugar.

gewusst: To make one litre of maple syrup you need a great deal of tree sap, about 40 litres.
Cats cannot taste sweetness at all.

teile.einleitung: Tarmed was the tariff used in Switzerland to bill outpatient medical services. It set out how much a consultation or an examination costs. From 2026 it was replaced by TARDOC and outpatient flat rates.
wichtigste: Tarmed applied to outpatient medical services.
It was used across Switzerland from 2004.
Every service was rated in tariff points.
The value of a tariff point differed by canton and contract.
Tarmed was a fee-for-service tariff.
Its successors are TARDOC and outpatient flat rates.

abschnitte.titel: One tariff for the whole of Switzerland
abschnitte.text: **Tarmed** governed how doctors' practices and **hospital outpatient departments** billed their outpatient services. Outpatient means that you go home again after the treatment. In 2004 Tarmed replaced the previous **cantonal doctors' tariffs** with one tariff for the whole of Switzerland. Tarmed was a **fee-for-service tariff**. Each individual service, for example five minutes of consultation or an examination, was billed separately.

abschnitte.titel: Tariff points and tariff point value
abschnitte.text: Every service was rated in **tariff points**. To get the price, you multiply the tariff points by the **tariff point value** in francs. An example: 40 tariff points times 0.95 francs makes 38 francs. The number of tariff points was the same across Switzerland, but the tariff point value was agreed regionally. So the same service did not cost the same everywhere.

Doctors' tariffs are negotiated first of all by the **tariff partners**. These are associations of doctors and hospitals on one side and the **insurers** on the other. Only if they cannot agree can the **Federal Council** step in. A different system applies to stays in hospitals for acute somatic care: since 2012, billing has used **SwissDRG** and **case-based flat rates**, that is a fixed amount depending on the diagnosis.

Over time Tarmed came to be seen as **out of date**, because medicine had changed a great deal. After long negotiations the Federal Council approved **TARDOC** and **outpatient flat rates** as successors. They replaced Tarmed from 2026. With flat rates, each individual service is no longer billed. Instead there is a fixed amount for a whole treatment.

gewusst: Every year, many millions of outpatient treatments in Switzerland were billed with Tarmed.
On a doctor's bill under Tarmed you could look up every single service with its tariff number.

teile.einleitung: The sympathetic nervous system is part of the autonomic nervous system. In times of stress and danger it prepares the body for action, without our controlling it consciously.
wichtigste: The sympathetic nervous system belongs to the autonomic nervous system.
It is especially active in times of stress and danger.
It speeds up the heartbeat and widens the pupils.
It widens the airways and slows down digestion.
The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline in the process.
The sympathetic trunk runs along both sides of the spine.

abschnitte.text: The **autonomic nervous system** controls the organs without our will, for example the heart, breathing and digestion. It consists of the **sympathetic nervous system**, the **parasympathetic nervous system** and the enteric nervous system of the gut. The sympathetic and parasympathetic systems mostly work as opposites. The sympathetic system is the accelerator, the parasympathetic system the brake for rest and recovery.

In times of stress and danger, the sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for **fight or flight**. It raises the **heart rate** and **blood pressure** so that the muscles get more blood. It widens the **airways** so that more air flows into the lungs. The **pupils** become wider so that more light enters the eye.

In a dangerous situation, digesting is not important. So the sympathetic nervous system **slows down** the activity of the stomach and gut. The flow of saliva also decreases, which is why your mouth goes dry when you are excited. The energy goes instead to the muscles, heart and brain.

On both sides of the spine runs a chain of nerve knots, the **sympathetic trunk**. There many sympathetic nerve fibres are switched over before they travel on to the organs. At the nerve endings the messenger substance **noradrenaline** is at work. In addition, the **adrenal medulla** releases **adrenaline** into the blood. It strengthens the effects of the sympathetic nervous system throughout the body.

gewusst: The sweat glands are also controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, which is why you sweat when you are excited.
The name comes from Greek and means roughly “feeling with”.

teile.einleitung: Sebaceous glands are small glands in the skin. They make sebum, a mixture of fats that keeps skin and hair supple and protects the skin.
wichtigste: Sebaceous glands make skin oil, called sebum.
Most of them open into the hair follicle.
There are no sebaceous glands on the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet.
There are especially many on the face, chest and back.
Sebaceous glands work holocrine: whole cells break down into sebum.
The Meibomian glands on the edge of the eyelid are special sebaceous glands.

abschnitte.text: **Sebum** is a mixture of different fats. Together with sweat it forms a thin **protective film** on the skin. This film keeps the skin supple, protects it from **drying out** and holds back many germs. Sebum also makes the hair soft and shiny.

Most sebaceous glands open into the **hair follicle**, the sheath around the hair. From there the sebum reaches the surface of the skin. The sebaceous glands of the scalp give off sebum constantly. It spreads along the hairs. That is why hair gets **greasy** if you do not wash it for a long time.

Especially many sebaceous glands sit on the **face**, above all in the so-called **T-zone** of forehead, nose and chin, and on the **chest**, the **back** and the scalp. There the skin gets shiny more quickly. On the **palms of the hands** and **soles of the feet**, by contrast, there are no hairs and no sebaceous glands either. In teenagers the glands often produce a lot of sebum, which can lead to spots.

Sebaceous glands work **holocrine**. This means that the gland cells fill up with fat, die and break down. Their whole contents become sebum. New cells grow back all the time. A special form is the **Meibomian glands** on the edge of the eyelids. They release fat into the tear film so that the tear fluid on the eye does not evaporate too quickly.

gewusst: On each eyelid, several dozen Meibomian glands sit side by side.
The word holocrine comes from Greek and means roughly “secreting entirely”.

teile.einleitung: Sugary drinks are drinks with a lot of added sugar, for example cola, lemonade or iced tea. They taste good, but often contain more sugar than you might think.
wichtigste: Half a litre of cola contains more than 10 sugar cubes.
Lemonade, cola and iced tea are sugary drinks.
Too much sugar can cause tooth decay.
Water and unsweetened tea are good ways to quench your thirst.
Squash should be diluted strongly with water.
Energy drinks are not suitable for children.

abschnitte.text: Half a litre of ordinary **cola** contains over 50 grams of sugar. That is more than **10 sugar cubes**. **Lemonade** and **iced tea** also contain a lot of added sugar. Because you cannot see the sugar in a drink, it is easy to drink a great deal of it. The fizzy bubbles in many sugary drinks come from **carbon dioxide**.

Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid. This acid attacks the teeth and can make holes, which is called **tooth decay**. People who often drink sugary drinks, especially in small sips throughout the day, are more likely to get tooth decay. Too much sugar can also contribute to being overweight.

The best thirst quencher is **water**. In Switzerland you can safely drink tap water. A slice of **lemon** or a few mint leaves give water flavour without much sugar. **Unsweetened herbal tea** contains no sugar either. **Squash** is very sweet, so you dilute it strongly with water.

**Energy drinks** contain a lot of **caffeine** and sugar. For children this is not healthy. It can cause, for example, a racing heart, restlessness and sleep problems. That is why energy drinks are not suitable for children. They are also not a sports drink and do not quench thirst well.

gewusst: Even fruit juices without added sugar contain a lot of natural fruit sugar.
Swiss tap water is one of the most closely monitored foods.

teile.einleitung: Tetanus, also known as lockjaw, is a dangerous disease caused by bacteria from the soil. They get into the body through wounds. A vaccination protects reliably.
wichtigste: Tetanus is also called lockjaw.
The bacteria live in the soil and in street dust.
A poison made by the bacteria causes severe muscle spasms.
Spasms of the jaw muscles are typical.
Tetanus does not pass from person to person.
Only your own vaccination protects you, even after you have had the illness.
Adults get a booster at the ages of 25, 45 and 65.

abschnitte.text: Tetanus is caused by the bacterium **Clostridium tetani**. It lives in the soil, in dust and in the gut of animals, and is present practically everywhere. The bacteria form very tough **spores** that can survive heat and dryness for years. If they get into the body through a dirty **wound**, they germinate. Even a small scratch while gardening can be enough.

The bacteria make a very powerful nerve poison, **tetanospasmin**. It disturbs the control of the muscles, which then cramp continuously. Tetanus often begins with **lockjaw**, so that you can hardly open your mouth. Later more muscles all over the body cramp. The illness has to be treated in hospital.

Tetanus is **not passed from person to person**. You only catch it through dirty wounds. That is why only your **own vaccination** protects you. Even someone who has survived tetanus is not immune afterwards. A tiny amount of poison is enough to cause the illness, but too little to build up protection. So you need a vaccination even after you have had the illness.

Children are vaccinated against tetanus as part of the **Swiss vaccination schedule**. For adults the **Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)** recommends boosters at the ages of **25, 45 and 65**, that is every 20 years, and after that every 10 years. The tetanus vaccination is usually given as a **combined vaccine** with **diphtheria**, often also with whooping cough. After an injury, the doctor checks whether the vaccine protection is still enough.

gewusst: Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburo developed an antiserum against tetanus around 1890.
Tetanus spores can survive in the soil for many years.

teile.einleitung: Synaesthesia is a special way of perceiving the world. One stimulus also sets off an impression in another sense. Some people, for example, see colours when they hear music.
wichtigste: In synaesthesia, sense impressions are linked together.
The Greek word means roughly feeling together.
A common form is grapheme-colour synaesthesia.
A few per cent of people have some form of it.
Synaesthesia is not regarded as an illness.
The links usually stay the same for years.

abschnitte.text: In **synaesthesia** two senses are connected with each other. A sound can set off a colour, a word a taste. The word is made up of the Greek “syn” for together and “aisthesis” for sensation. So it means **feeling together**. What is meant is the shared sensing of several senses.

A common form is **grapheme-colour synaesthesia**. A **grapheme** is a written character. People with it might, for example, always see the letter A as red or the number 7 as green. These links stay the **same** for many years. Someone who sees the 5 as blue will still see it as blue years later. Researchers use this consistency as a test for genuine synaesthesia.

Studies estimate that **a few per cent** of people have synaesthetic perceptions. Many do not even know that this is something special, because for them it has always been that way. Synaesthesia runs in some families. So it is thought that **genes** play a part. Today synaesthesia is regarded as a special way of perceiving, **not as an illness**, and it needs no treatment.

The painter **Wassily Kandinsky** is often linked with synaesthesia. He described experiencing sounds as colours, and he translated music into colours and shapes. Many of his abstract paintings have titles from music, such as “Composition” or “Improvisation”. Many people with synaesthesia find their perception to be an enrichment.

gewusst: Two people with synaesthesia usually see the same letter in quite different colours.
Some people with synaesthesia can remember numbers especially well thanks to their colours.

teile.einleitung: Sweets such as chocolate (known as “Schoggi” in Swiss German), boiled sweets or biscuits taste delicious and bring joy. But they contain a lot of sugar. So the rule is: enjoy them, but in small amounts, and brush your teeth afterwards.
wichtigste: Sweets contain a lot of sugar.
In Switzerland sugar is made from sugar beet.
The food pyramid recommends at most one small portion of sweet things a day.
You should brush your teeth after sweets.
Bees make honey from nectar.
“Schoggi” is the Swiss German word for chocolate.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss food pyramid** shows how much of which foods you should eat. At the bottom are drinks, vegetables and fruit, of which you need plenty. **Sweet things** are at the narrow **tip**. You may enjoy them, but only a small portion a day. After sweets you should **brush your teeth**, so that no sugar is left behind and no tooth decay develops.

In Switzerland sugar is made from **sugar beet**. The beets grow in fields on the Central Plateau and are processed in the sugar factories in **Aarberg** and **Frauenfeld**. A natural sweet food is **honey**. Bees collect nectar from flowers and make it into honey, which contains a lot of sugar.

Switzerland is famous for its **“Schoggi”**, which is what people say in Swiss German for chocolate. Boiled sweets are called **“Zältli”** and biscuits **“Guetzli”**. From Basel come the **Basler Läckerli**, small, hard gingerbread biscuits with honey and spices. **Meringues** are white, airy bakes made from whisked egg white and sugar. They are especially well known in the Bernese Oberland, where people like to eat them with cream.

If you fancy something sweet, you can also reach for **fruit**. It contains natural sugar, but also vitamins and fibre. Dried fruit such as dates or apricots is also sweet, but sticks to the teeth. It is best to eat sweets after a meal and not all day long.

gewusst: The village of Meiringen in the Bernese Oberland is often named as the home of meringues.
Switzerland is one of the countries where the most chocolate per person is eaten.

teile.einleitung: Systole is the phase of the heartbeat in which the ventricles contract and pump blood into the body. It is followed by diastole, in which the heart relaxes and fills up again.
wichtigste: Systole means contraction in Greek.
In systole the ventricles pump blood into the large arteries.
It begins with the tensing phase, followed by the ejection phase.
During ejection the aortic and pulmonary valves are open.
At the start of systole you hear the first heart sound.
In systole the pressure in the aorta is at its highest.

abschnitte.text: The word **systole** comes from Greek and means **contraction**. That is exactly what the heart muscle does in this phase. The muscle of the **ventricles** contracts and presses the blood into the large arteries: the left ventricle into the **aorta**, the right into the pulmonary artery. This is followed by **diastole**, in which the muscle relaxes and the ventricles fill up again.

Heart valves work like valves in a pipe and make sure that blood flows in one direction only. During ejection the **semilunar valves** at the exits of the ventricles open, that is the **aortic and pulmonary valves**. The **atrioventricular valves** to the atria are closed so that no blood flows back.

At the start the ventricle muscle tenses, but all the valves are briefly closed. In this **tensing phase** no blood flows out yet, only the pressure rises. As soon as the pressure in the ventricle is higher than in the artery, the valve opens. Now the **ejection phase** begins, and the blood streams out.

At the start of systole the atrioventricular valves close and the heart muscle tenses. This produces the **first heart sound**, which you hear with a stethoscope. When the left ventricle ejects blood, the pressure in the aorta rises to its peak. This **systolic blood pressure** is the first, higher number when blood pressure is measured. An **extrasystole** is an additional, premature heartbeat. Occasional extrasystoles are common and usually harmless.

gewusst: With a blood pressure of 120 over 80, 120 is the systolic value.
The second heart sound is produced when the semilunar valves close at the end of systole.

teile.einleitung: You need a handkerchief to blow your nose, above all when you have a cold. In Switzerland people often call it a “Nastuch”. Used properly, it helps to stop germs from being passed on.
wichtigste: In Switzerland a handkerchief is often called a “Nastuch”.
Disposable tissues are made of soft paper.
You use a paper tissue only once.
You blow one nostril after the other.
After blowing your nose you wash your hands.
Used tissues contain germs.

abschnitte.text: It is best to blow **one nostril after the other**. You hold one nostril closed and blow gently through the other. That way you do not push the mucus into your ears. With a **cold** your nose often runs, and then you need a lot of tissues. Afterwards you **wash your hands**, because germs get onto your fingers when you blow your nose.

**Disposable tissues** are made of soft, absorbent paper. That is why they are also called **paper handkerchiefs**. They are meant for **single use**. For the next time you take a fresh one and throw the old one in the bin. In the past, people mainly used handkerchiefs made of **cloth**, which are washed again and again. In Switzerland a handkerchief is often called a **“Nastuch”**.

There can be **viruses** and **bacteria** in nasal mucus. That is why you do not touch other people's used tissues, otherwise you can catch something. If you do not have a tissue to hand, it is best to sneeze or cough into the **crook of your elbow** instead of into your hand. That way fewer germs end up on door handles or toys.

To have fresh tissues with you when you are out and about, you put a small **pack** in your pocket or school bag. The pack keeps the tissues clean and dry. You can take it anywhere, to school, on trips or to training.

gewusst: A used paper tissue belongs in the rubbish bin, not in the waste paper.
When you sneeze, the air can shoot out of the nose and mouth at great speed.

teile.einleitung: A tattoo is a picture or pattern that is pricked into the skin with ink so that it lasts for good. People have been tattooing themselves for thousands of years. Because the skin is injured in the process, a fresh tattoo needs care.
wichtigste: The ink is pricked into the dermis.
Scavenger cells take up the ink and hold on to it.
Ötzi has more than 60 tattoos.
The word tattoo comes from Polynesia.
Among the Māori, face tattoos have a long tradition.
Tattoos are usually removed with a laser.

abschnitte.text: When tattooing, a fine needle pricks the skin very many times and brings ink in as it does so. The ink has to reach the **dermis**, the layer under the outer skin. If it lay only in the **epidermis**, it would flake off after a few weeks, because this layer constantly renews itself. In the dermis, **scavenger cells**, also called macrophages, take up the particles of ink. Because they cannot break them down, the picture stays visible.

The glacier mummy **Ötzi** from the Ötztal Alps is over 5,000 years old. More than 60 tattoos made of lines and crosses were found on his skin. The word “tattoo” goes back to **“tatau”** from Tahiti in Polynesia. Sailors around **James Cook** brought it to Europe in the 18th century. Among the **Māori** in New Zealand the traditional tattoos are called **Tā moko**. They show a person's origin and standing.

In tattooing the skin is injured thousands of times. A fresh tattoo is therefore a **wound** that first has to heal. Until then you should not go swimming and should not expose the tattoo to the sun. Germs in the water can cause infections, and sunlight can damage the ink. Later on, too, sun cream protects the tattoo from fading.

A **henna tattoo** is a painted design that disappears after a while. Henna only stains the upper layers of the skin and fades after a few weeks. There are warnings about so-called “black henna” with added substances, because it can cause allergies. A real tattoo is today usually removed with a **laser**. The light breaks up the particles of ink, which the body then gradually clears away. This usually takes several sessions.

gewusst: Ötzi's tattoos are often on joints and on the back. Researchers suspect that they may have been used to treat pain.
Removing a tattoo usually takes much longer and costs more than getting it.

teile.einleitung: A syncope is a brief faint. You lose consciousness for a few seconds because the brain briefly gets too little blood, and you usually recover quickly afterwards.
wichtigste: Syncope is the technical term for a brief faint.
The cause is a short reduction of blood flow to the brain.
A faint usually lasts only seconds to a few minutes.
Standing for a long time in great heat can bring on a faint.
Your vision going black is a typical warning sign.
You lay the person flat and raise their legs.

abschnitte.text: In a **syncope**, the brain briefly gets too little blood. As a result it lacks oxygen, and you lose consciousness for a moment. The term comes from Greek. Typically you come round again by yourself after seconds or a few minutes. If the unconsciousness lasts longer, medical help is needed.

A faint happens especially easily when **standing for a long time in great heat**. The blood vessels widen, and blood collects in the legs. Some people faint at the sight of blood or when they are in pain. In this **vasovagal syncope** the nervous system reacts too strongly, and pulse and blood pressure suddenly drop.

Before a faint, **dizziness**, **blackouts of vision**, nausea and sweating often appear. If you notice this, it is best to sit or lie down straight away. That way you can avoid a fall. It also helps to drink enough and to move your leg muscles when standing for a long time.

If someone has fainted briefly and is breathing normally, you lay the person **flat** and **raise their legs**. This lets more blood flow to the heart and the brain, and usually the person comes round quickly. If the person stays unconscious but breathes normally, you put them in the **recovery position**. This keeps the airways clear. Then you call for help, in Switzerland the ambulance service on **144**, and check the breathing.

gewusst: Most faints are harmless, but a first faint should still be checked by a doctor.
If you have to stand for a long time, you can guard against fainting by tensing your leg muscles again and again.

teile.einleitung: Suva is the largest accident insurer in Switzerland. It mainly insures employees in industry, trades and construction against accidents and occupational diseases, and works hard to prevent accidents.
wichtigste: Suva stands for Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund.
Its head office is in Lucerne.
It covers accidents at work, accidents outside work and occupational diseases.
From 8 hours a week, leisure accidents are insured too.
The daily allowance is 80 per cent of the insured earnings.
Suva returns surpluses through lower premiums.
Prevention, insurance and rehabilitation are its three pillars.

abschnitte.text: **Suva**, the **Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund**, has its head office in **Lucerne** and agencies all over Switzerland. It is an independent organisation under public law and **not profit-oriented**. It returns surpluses to the insured people as lower premiums. Those insured are mainly employees in industry, trades and construction.

The compulsory accident insurance under the **Accident Insurance Act** (UVG) covers accidents at work, accidents in leisure time and **occupational diseases**. Ordinary illnesses are covered by health insurance. Anyone who works **at least eight hours a week** for the same employer is also insured for leisure accidents. Below that, only accidents at work are covered.

The accident insurance pays the treatment costs. If someone cannot work, there is a **daily allowance**. In the case of full incapacity for work it is **80 per cent** of the insured earnings and is paid out after a short waiting period. Suva runs two **rehabilitation clinics**: in **Bellikon** in the canton of Aargau and in **Sion** in the Valais. There people who have had accidents learn to return to everyday life and work.

Besides insurance, Suva takes care of **prevention**. It advises companies, checks workplace safety in many industries and runs campaigns, including on leisure accidents in sport. Prevention, insurance and rehabilitation are its three pillars.

The highest governing body is the **Suva Council** with 40 seats. 16 belong to employers' organisations, 16 to employees' organisations and 8 to the federal government. The members are elected by the **Federal Council** for four years. In this way employers, employees and the federal government decide on Suva together.

gewusst: At Suva, employers and employees sit at the same table with equal strength.
Apprentices are also insured against accidents through their company from their very first day of work.

teile.einleitung: The thalamus is an important relay station deep in the brain. Almost all sensory stimuli pass through it before they reach the cerebral cortex. It filters what we become aware of.
wichtigste: The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon.
It filters sensory information and passes it on to the cerebral cortex.
It is also called the “gateway to consciousness”.
Only the sense of smell does not mainly run through the thalamus.
The lateral geniculate nucleus passes signals from the retina to the visual cortex.
The Greek “thalamos” means chamber or bedchamber.

abschnitte.text: The **thalamus** is the largest part of the **diencephalon**. It lies deep inside, between the cerebrum and the brainstem. There are two of them, one in each half of the brain. The name comes from the Greek “thalamos”, which meant an inner room or **bedchamber**. This fits its hidden position deep in the brain.

Almost all sensory stimuli pass through the thalamus on their way to the **cerebral cortex**. It is a **relay station** and filters which information is important. That is why it is also called the “gateway to consciousness”. Only the **sense of smell** is an exception. Smell information travels from the olfactory bulb directly to the olfactory cortex, without first being switched over in the thalamus.

The thalamus is made up of many groups of nerve cells, the **nuclei**. Each has its own jobs. The **lateral geniculate nucleus** receives the fibres of the optic nerve. From there the visual pathways run to the **visual cortex** in the occipital lobe. Other nuclei pass on signals from hearing, touch or taste, or help to control movements.

After a **stroke** in the thalamus, **Dejerine-Roussy syndrome** can develop. People with it suffer severe pain on the opposite side of the body. In the very rare **fatal familial insomnia**, misfolded proteins called prions destroy mainly nuclei of the thalamus. In **essential tremor** the hands shake. In this **deep brain stimulation**, an electrode in a nucleus of the thalamus can greatly reduce the shaking.

gewusst: The thalamus is also involved in sleep and helps to block out stimuli while you sleep.
Because almost all sensory pathways run through it, even small damage in the thalamus can disturb feeling or sight.

teile.einleitung: Theodor Kocher was a surgeon from Bern and one of the most famous doctors in Switzerland. He became known above all for his operations on the thyroid gland. In 1909 he became the first Swiss person to win the Nobel Prize.
wichtigste: Theodor Kocher lived from 1841 to 1917 and came from Bern.
From 1872 he headed the surgical clinic at the Inselspital in Bern.
He operated on thousands of people with goitre, an enlarged thyroid gland.
He cut the death rate in goitre operations to under one per cent.
In 1909 he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
The collar incision, the Kocher clamp and a manoeuvre for the shoulder are named after him.

abschnitte.text: Kocher studied medicine in Bern and trained further in several countries. At just 31 he became **professor of surgery** in Bern and headed the clinic at the **Inselspital**. He received offers from universities abroad, but stayed in Bern. There he worked until his death in 1917.

In Kocher's time very many people in Switzerland had a **goitre**. The reason was **iodine deficiency**: in the Alpine regions the soil and water contain little iodine. Without iodine the thyroid gland in the neck becomes enlarged. A large goitre can press on the windpipe and make breathing difficult. Kocher developed safe operations for such cases.

Kocher worked very precisely and took care over thorough **control of bleeding** and over **asepsis**, that is working free of germs. As a result the death rate in goitre operations fell from very high levels to **under one per cent**. For access he chose a crosswise **collar incision** in a fold of skin on the neck, the scar of which is hardly noticeable later.

Kocher observed that people whose whole thyroid gland had been removed later became sluggish, clumsy and mentally slowed. From this he realised that the **thyroid gland is vital**. After that he always left a remnant of the gland in place during operations. For his work on the thyroid gland he received the **Nobel Prize** in 1909.

Many things in medicine bear Kocher's name. The **Kocher clamp** is a clamp with toothed tips, used to grip tissue and blood vessels. It is still used today. With the **Kocher manoeuvre** a dislocated shoulder is put back into place by turning and guiding the arm in a fixed sequence.

gewusst: Kocher was the first surgeon in the world to receive a Nobel Prize.
In Bern, the Theodor Kocher Institute of the university commemorates him.

teile.einleitung: A synapse is the point of contact where one nerve cell passes a signal on to the next cell. Most often this happens with chemical messenger substances that jump across a tiny gap. Our brain has an unimaginably large number of such connections, and they change constantly as we learn.
wichtigste: At a synapse, signals are passed from one nerve cell to the next.
Most often this happens through chemical messenger substances, the neurotransmitters.
Between the two cells lies a tiny gap, the synaptic cleft.
The brain has many trillions of synapses.
When we learn, synapses are strengthened or newly formed.
Some medicines and poisons act directly on the synapses.
The term synapse was coined around 1897 by the British researcher Charles Sherrington.

abschnitte.text: Nerve cells, also called **neurons**, pass on information as electrical signals. At the end of their long extension, the axon, they meet another cell. This point of contact is called a **synapse**. The other cell can be another nerve cell, a muscle cell or a gland cell. The word comes from Greek and means connection.

The two cells do not touch. Between them lies the **synaptic cleft**, much thinner than a hair. When an electrical signal arrives at the end of the first cell, it releases messenger substances from small sacs. These **neurotransmitters** travel across the gap. On the other side they dock onto matching **receptors** like a key in a lock. This creates a new electrical signal in the next cell.

There are many different neurotransmitters with different jobs. **Acetylcholine** gives muscles the command to contract. **Dopamine** plays a part in reward and motivation. Serotonin influences mood and sleep. Some messenger substances stimulate the next cell, others slow it down.

A human brain has around 86 billion nerve cells. Each of them can be connected to thousands of others through synapses. When we practise something, the synapses involved become stronger, which is called **synaptic plasticity**. Connections that are rarely used, on the other hand, are broken down. In this way the brain changes throughout life.

Many medicines act on the synapses, for example some drugs for depression or pain. Poisons also attack here. The arrow poison **curare** blocks the synapses between nerves and muscles, so that the muscles are paralysed. Caffeine and nicotine also affect signal transmission. In illnesses such as Parkinson's disease, there is too little of the messenger substance dopamine in certain parts of the brain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A nerve cell that passes on electrical signals.
A chemical messenger substance that carries signals across a synapse.
The tiny space between two cells at a synapse.
A docking point to which a matching messenger substance binds.

gewusst: Besides chemical synapses there are also electrical synapses, where the signal flows directly from cell to cell.
Toddlers have more synapses than adults, and unused ones are broken down later.
Transmission at a chemical synapse takes only about a thousandth of a second.
